problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+49{y}^{2}=196,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

activity_context.topic_title: Line Integrals of Scalar Functions Over Ellipses

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061629/assets/78f8ca3e70afb8377748a18d7024ba297e330add59550a41a87025a0145b56bb.png)

Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}9xy\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4$  traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,1).$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=18\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}9xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}18\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2({4}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =2(8-1) \\  & =14\end{aligned}
$$
